My sister always had such a green thumb, you know, she could make anything grow, even those frightfully difficult little ferns. These are from some distant clime, I imagine. One hears such tales of Captain Thorne’s travels, does one not? He always brings back the most extraordinary things for his sister, though she cares for nothing but her needlework, poor dear. Do you suppose these were sent from abroad, Miss Finch? Or merely from London, which can be quite foreign enough to me sometimes.”

Mr. Hartley, seeing Miss Finch about to attempt a reply to this delightful meandering, quickly intervened. “Indeed, Mrs. Gable, one might almost imagine them to have arrived on the very ship that brought Captain Thorne himself. Is not that the one, Miss Arabella, that sailed from the Indies but a fortnight past? I trust the sea air has done them no lasting harm.” Arabella glanced sharply at him, her forced composure momentarily broken. “I have no knowledge of any such vessel, Mr. Hartley. And a truly singular generosity, I understand.” Miss Vance now caught a swift, almost imperceptible glance between Miss Finch and Mr. Hartley, a flash of something shared, perhaps conspiratorial, that deepened her earlier amusement into a more definite suspicion. This was not merely playful banter; there was a meaning beneath, a private language, the significance of which only they, it seemed, fully comprehended.

Mr. Thorne, how delightful! We were just speaking of you, were we not, Miss Finch? And your sister, too. Do come in, pray, and tell us if you have seen anything of the Colonel today. My poor dear cousin, Mrs. Plumley, has been expecting him for her whist party since Tuesday last.” Mr. Thorne, with a polite but firm nod, acknowledged Mrs. Gable, but his gaze, quite directly, sought Miss Finch. “Miss Arabella, I trust the plants are thriving? I confess I worried about their journey. Were the instructions regarding their care clear enough?” His tone was not reproachful, but entirely earnest, and it cut through the room’s previous ambiguities with the clarity of a freshly sharpened blade. Miss Finch’s colour deepened once more, a much more vivid blush this time, and she stammered, “Perfectly clear, Mr. Thorne, and they are doing quite well, I assure you. Most excellent, indeed.” Miss Vance exchanged a quick glance with Mr. Hartley, whose amused smile, though carefully controlled, now held a definite hint of triumph.

I have been thinking of you a great deal, and I wished very much to speak with you.” She sat down beside her, her voice gentle, yet firm. “I am afraid you have been very unhappy, my poor friend, and I feel, with a bitterness I can scarcely express, that I have been greatly to blame.”

Harriet looked up, her blue eyes wide with bewilderment. “To blame, Emma? Oh, no! You have always been so kind to me, so very good.”

“No, Harriet, not always good,” Emma corrected, shaking her head. “I have been, in many respects, very foolish, and my folly has led you into distress. You have too good a heart to see the faults of those who profess to be your friends, and I fear I have taken advantage of that goodness. I have been presumptuous, and I have led your affections astray.”

Harriet’s eyes filled with tears, and she quickly turned her head away. “Oh, Emma, please do not say so. If there has been any mistake, it is all my own doing. I have been so very silly.”

“No, Harriet, you have been misled,” Emma insisted, her voice full of earnest penitence. “I persuaded you, against your better judgement, against the clear promptings of your own good sense, to attach yourself where there was no prospect of return, and where, I now see, there was no true desert. I filled your head with notions of consequence and expectation that were utterly groundless. It was wrong of me, deeply wrong, and I cannot forgive myself for the pain I have caused you.”

She paused, allowing her words to sink in. Harriet was weeping quietly now, her face buried in her hands. Emma reached out and gently stroked her arm. “My dear Harriet, it grieves me beyond measure to see you so distressed, but it is better that the truth be faced, however painful it may be. Mr. Frank Churchill, we now know, has been for some time secretly engaged to Miss Fairfax. All his attentions, all his seeming preferences, were but a part of a necessary deception, a sad means to an end. He was bound by honour, or by what he conceived to be honour, to another.”

Harriet raised her head, her face tear-stained, but a spark of dawning comprehension in her eyes. “Secretly engaged?” she whispered. “To Miss Fairfax? But he always seemed to, to enjoy my company so very much.”

“He is a man of easy manners, Harriet, and of universal gallantry,” Emma explained, choosing her words carefully, for she did not wish to denigrate Frank Churchill more than was strictly necessary, especially given her own past blindness. “He has a way of pleasing all, and in his situation, it was perhaps unavoidable that his attentions should be misinterpreted by many. But my fault lay in encouraging you to misinterpret them, in leading you to believe that such pleasantness could only spring from a deeper regard.”

“And all those conversations, all those little looks and words,” Harriet murmured, almost to herself. “They meant nothing?”

“They meant, I imagine, that he wished to be agreeable, as any well-bred gentleman would,” Emma said, gently. “But they did not mean that his heart was free, or that his intentions towards you were serious. That was my unhappy invention, Harriet, and I must beg your forgiveness for it. I was foolish, I was presumptuous, and I have brought you to this sorrow.”

Harriet, after a few moments of silent weeping, at length found her voice, though it was still tremulous. “You are too good, Emma, to blame yourself so freely. I should have known better. I should have listened to my own heart, which, I own, sometimes felt a little uneasy, even when you were most encouraging.” She looked directly at Emma, a new earnestness in her gaze. “But what am I to do now? My mind feels quite lost. All my hopes, all my little dreams…”

“You must gather them up, my dear, and set them upon a more secure foundation,” Emma advised, her own sense of direction having at last found a steady compass. “Your heart is good, Harriet, and capable of great affection. But it must be bestowed where it is truly appreciated, and where it can meet with an open and honest return. This disappointment, painful as it is, will in time pass. You are young, and your future is still before you. And you have friends who love you very much, and who will always wish for your happiness.”

Harriet wiped her eyes with her handkerchief. “I know you do, Emma. And I am very grateful. I have felt so very lonely these past days, and so confused.”

“You must not feel lonely,” Emma declared, with warmth. “You must come to Hartfield more often. We will find ways to divert your mind, and you will see that this sorrow, though now it feels immense, will diminish, and new joys will arise. And, Harriet,” she continued, with a careful sincerity, “I must also speak to you about another matter, a subject I know we have discussed before, and where again, my advice was most lamentably misguided. I mean Mr. Martin.”

Harriet’s face coloured deeply, and she looked down at her hands. “Mr. Martin,” she repeated, in a barely audible voice.

“Yes, Mr. Martin,” Emma persisted, with resolute frankness. “I fear I prevailed upon you to reject a very worthy man, a man of integrity and good character, whose attachment to you was sincere and steady. I painted him in colours that were unjust, and I encouraged you to aspire to a situation which, in truth, could never have brought you happiness. I was wrong, Harriet, utterly wrong. Mr. Martin, I have come to see, is in every respect a most eligible connection for you, and a man who would, I am certain, make you a most excellent husband.”

Harriet remained silent, her blushes deepening, her hands clasped tightly in her lap. Emma waited, allowing her words to sink in. She knew that such a reversal of counsel would be startling, perhaps even shocking, but it was a truth she felt bound to speak.

At length, Harriet raised her head again, her eyes still downcast, but a faint, timid smile playing about her lips. “He was always so very kind to me, Emma. And his sisters are very good girls.”

“Indeed they are,” Emma agreed, her heart lightening with a hopeful anticipation. “And he himself is a man of sound sense and true feeling. He has a solid home, a respectable profession, and a steadiness of temper which would ensure your domestic felicity. I spoke ill of him, Harriet, from a foolish pride and an unwarranted estimation of worldly advantages. I see my error now, and I implore you to reconsider him, if, as I believe, his regard for you has not entirely diminished.”

Harriet did not reply directly, but her silence, combined with the gentle colour in her cheeks, spoke volumes. Emma felt a surge of genuine relief. It was a beginning, a first step towards undoing the mischief she had created. She spent another hour with Harriet, offering comfort, gently turning her thoughts towards more realistic prospects, and reiterating her sincere affection and desire for her friend’s well-being. By the time she took her leave, Harriet, though still sorrowful, seemed lighter, her spirits perceptibly, if subtly, lifted. Emma herself felt a measure of peace, knowing she had, at last, begun to set right her wrongs.

Returning to Hartfield, Emma’s reflections were naturally coloured by the events of the morning. She had humbled herself, confessed her errors, and attempted to guide Harriet towards a truer path. The relief was immense, but it was accompanied by a renewed sense of how much more she had yet to learn, how much more her character required refinement. Her thoughts turned, inevitably, to Mr. Knightley. His unwavering good sense, his clear-sightedness, his unwavering rectitude, these qualities, which she had so often dismissed as censorious, now shone with an almost irresistible brilliance. She longed for his approbation, for his understanding, and, most ardently, for his affection. But to hope for the latter, after her long resistance and ungrateful indifference, felt presumptuous. She could only strive to be worthy, to prove by her future conduct that she was at last learning to discern true merit, and to cultivate that humility which alone could make her estimable in his eyes.

The remainder of the day passed quietly at Hartfield. Mr. Woodhouse, seeing Emma somewhat restored by her walk and her conversation, was in good spirits, and the evening was spent in the customary placid enjoyment of their home. Emma, however, found her mind restless. She wished for some new development, some sign, some occasion to further test her resolve and perhaps, just perhaps, to bring her into closer contact with Mr. Knightley.

The opportunity, though not precisely what she might have contrived, arrived the very next morning in the form of an urgent message from Mrs. Weston. Emma, upon reading it, felt a mixed sensation of surprise and a peculiar dread.

“My dearest Emma,” the letter began, in Mrs. Weston’s hurried, yet elegant hand, “you will, I am sure, have already heard of the extraordinary revelations of the past few days. The secrecy of Mr. Frank Churchill’s engagement to Miss Fairfax, so long maintained, and now so unexpectedly brought to light, has created a considerable stir here at Randalls, and indeed, throughout the neighbourhood. Mr. Weston is quite in a fever of spirits, alternating between self-reproach for his blindness and a proud satisfaction in his son’s choice.

But it is not merely this news that compels me to write. We have just received a further communication from Mr. Churchill, by way of his Aunt, Mrs. Churchill. Alas, my dear Emma, I must convey to you tidings of the utmost distress. Mrs. Churchill, whose health has been so long precarious, has, I grieve to say, passed away quite suddenly. She was taken ill only two days ago, and despite every possible attention, her strength failed her. Mr. Churchill is, naturally, in a state of profound shock and sorrow.

He sends his love to us all, but particularly wishes for his parents not to undertake the journey to Enscombe at this difficult time, preferring to be alone with his uncle. He also wishes for Miss Fairfax to be apprised of the melancholy event, and begs that she should not feel obliged to wait upon him. His return to Highbury, which we had so happily anticipated, is now, of course, indefinitely postponed.

My dear Emma, I know what a shock this will be to you, and to all of us. Mr. Frank Churchill, though sometimes thoughtless, is a young man of considerable parts, and this heavy blow must be felt keenly. I hope you will come to us as soon as you can, if only for a quiet morning, that we may talk over these sad events. I am very anxious, too, about poor Miss Fairfax. How she will bear such a complication of events, I cannot tell. The joy of her engagement overshadowed by such a bereavement! Mr. Knightley, I know, will be calling this afternoon. Perhaps you might be able to join us. Your presence would be a great comfort to me.

With the fondest regards,
Yours ever,
Anne Weston.”

Emma read the letter through twice, her emotions a complex tangle. Grief for Mrs. Churchill, though she had never known her, was certainly present, a respectful sorrow for the loss of a life. But more immediate was the consideration of how this event would impact those around her, particularly Frank Churchill and, by extension, Jane Fairfax. The unexpected death freed Frank from his dependence on his aunt, removing the primary obstacle to his marriage. This, she knew, would ultimately simplify matters for him and Jane, though it came at such a heavy cost.

Her own feelings for Frank Churchill, which had so lately undergone such a profound and painful alteration, were now a curious mixture of residual affection, pity for his present sorrow, and a sense of detachment. She could not pretend to the passionate concern she might once have felt, for the truth of his character, as she now understood it, precluded such a sentiment. Yet, she wished him well, and sincerely commiserated with his loss.

Her immediate concern, however, turned to Jane Fairfax. How would the reserved and sensitive Jane bear this sudden shift in her fortunes, from the clandestine joy of her engagement to the public revelation, followed almost immediately by the death of her fiancé’s aunt, the very person whose disfavor they had so feared? Emma felt a genuine pang of sympathy for her, recognizing the immense pressure Jane must now be under.

She showed the letter to her father, who was predictably distressed by the news of Mrs. Churchill’s demise. He lamented the fragility of human life, and spoke at length of the perils of travel and the importance of a warm house, as if these considerations might somehow mitigate the suddenness of such an event. Emma patiently listened, offering suitable words of condolence, and then made her arrangements to visit Randalls that afternoon, as Mrs. Weston had requested. The prospect of seeing Mr. Knightley there, though not explicitly stated in Mrs. Weston’s invitation, was an added, if unspoken, impetus.

Upon her arrival at Randalls, she found Mrs. Weston indeed looking pale and anxious. Mr. Weston was pacing the drawing-room, still flushed with the agitation of the news.

“My dear Emma,” Mrs. Weston exclaimed, rising to embrace her. “How good of you to come. I have been so wishing for a quiet conversation. This dreadful news! And following so closely upon the other! My head feels quite in a whirl.”

Mr. Weston greeted her with a mournful shake of his head. “A sad business, Emma, a very sad business. Poor Isabella’s aunt! So unexpected. Frank will be quite heartbroken. And to think, only a few days ago, we were all congratulating ourselves on the impending marriage. Life, my dear, is full of such turns.”

“Indeed it is, Mr. Weston,” Emma replied, taking a seat. “My sincerest condolences. It is a very sudden and shocking event.”

“And poor Jane Fairfax!” Mrs. Weston sighed. “What a situation for her. To have her engagement at last revealed, and then immediately plunged into such mourning. She is so delicate, so very sensitive. I called upon her this morning, but she was quite overcome. I fear she is suffering greatly.”

“I can well imagine it,” Emma said, with genuine sympathy. “Her sensibilities are very acute. And it is a situation that would try the strongest constitution.”

“Mr. Knightley will be here soon,” Mr. Weston announced, glancing at the clock. “He sent word he would come after his business in Kingston. He is very concerned for Frank, naturally, and for Miss Fairfax too, I believe. He has always had a just appreciation of her worth.”

At the mention of Mr. Knightley, Emma’s heart gave a little flutter. She hoped he would indeed come, and that she might find an opportunity to speak with him, perhaps even to convey, in some subtle way, the change that had taken place within her.

It was not long before a carriage was heard approaching, and soon after, Mr. Knightley was ushered into the room. He greeted them all with a quiet gravity, his countenance reflecting the sombreness of the occasion. His eyes, as they met Emma’s, held a deeper scrutiny than usual, a look of kind concern that made her own gaze falter for a moment.

“This is indeed a melancholy time,” Mr. Knightley began, accepting a cup of tea from Mrs. Weston. “Poor Mrs. Churchill. Though I never had the pleasure of her acquaintance, I know her loss will be keenly felt by her husband and her nephew. And it brings with it such profound changes for others.”

“Indeed it does,” Mrs. Weston assented. “My heart aches for poor Jane. To have her happy prospects so quickly mingled with such sorrow. She is at once liberated and burdened.”

Mr. Knightley nodded slowly. “It is a cruel irony, Mrs. Weston. But perhaps, in time, it will prove to be a blessing in disguise for them both. Frank Churchill, I imagine, will now be master of his own fortune, and at liberty to marry without delay. Though he will doubtless feel the loss of his aunt very deeply, the removal of the necessity for concealment must be a great relief to him and Miss Fairfax.”

Emma listened attentively to Mr. Knightley’s calm and sensible assessment. There was no trace of triumph or superiority in his voice, only a compassionate understanding of the complexities of the situation. She found herself admiring him more than ever.

“It is true,” Emma ventured, speaking for the first time since Mr. Knightley’s arrival. “The freedom to act openly must, in the long run, be a comfort to them. Though the manner of its arrival is so sad.”

Mr. Knightley looked at her, and his eyes, though still serious, held a softer expression. “You speak very justly, Emma. To live under such constraint, to maintain such a prolonged deception, must have been a great strain upon them both. Especially upon Miss Fairfax, whose character, though reserved, is, I believe, fundamentally upright.”

Emma felt a blush rise to her cheeks. She knew that he, above all others, had suspected the truth, or at least had been least deceived by Frank Churchill’s stratagems. And she, in her folly, had been the most vocal in her disbelief, the most resistant to his wisdom. Her recent visit to Harriet had deepened her sense of penitence on this score.

“I confess, Mr. Knightley,” she said, her voice a little subdued, “I have been very blind in this matter, and very much mistaken in my judgements. I regret having misconstrued so many things, and having been so slow to perceive the truth.”

Mr. Knightley’s gaze softened further. He did not immediately reply, but merely looked at her, a profound, almost tender understanding in his eyes. It was a look that conveyed forgiveness, a silent acknowledgment of her self-correction, and it brought a warmth to Emma’s heart that was almost overwhelming. She felt herself understood, truly and deeply understood, without the need for further explanation or apology.

Mr. Weston, perhaps sensing a delicate moment, or simply restless in his grief, then diverted the conversation to the specifics of Mrs. Churchill’s will, and the probable impact on Frank Churchill’s inheritance. Emma joined in the general discussion, but her mind was still lingering on Mr. Knightley’s look, on the quiet assurance it had given her.

Later in the afternoon, as Mr. Weston had briefly left the room, and Mrs. Weston was engaged in writing a sympathetic note to Frank Churchill, Mr. Knightley found a moment to speak to Emma alone, though within earshot.

“I was glad to hear you speak as you did just now, Emma,” he said, his voice low, but clear. “It shews a candour and a humility that do you great credit. It is not always easy to admit one has been mistaken, especially when one’s errors have led to… regrettable consequences for others.”

Emma knew he was alluding to Harriet. She looked at him, her heart full. “Indeed, Mr. Knightley, it has been a very painful lesson. I have been foolish, presumptuous, and in many ways, quite unpardonably arrogant. I fear I have caused a great deal of unhappiness, not least to my poor Harriet.”

“Harriet is a good girl, Emma,” he replied, with a gentle tone. “And your friendship, however misguided it may sometimes have been, has always been founded on genuine affection. I believe she will recover from this, and perhaps, with proper guidance, will find her way to a more suitable happiness.” He paused, then added, with a subtle emphasis, “I have always believed she was capable of discerning true worth, if only her judgement were not swayed by false notions.”

Emma understood his meaning perfectly. He was encouraging her, subtly reinforcing her own efforts with Harriet. “I have endeavoured this morning to set her mind to rights, so far as I am able,” she confessed, her voice earnest. “I have told her of my errors, and tried to persuade her to a different view of things. I hope I have not been too late.”

A faint smile touched Mr. Knightley’s lips. “I have no doubt that your influence, now rightly directed, will be very efficacious, Emma. You have a great power over her, and it is a power I now trust you will wield for her true good.” He then looked away, as if considering something, before turning back to her. “This entire episode, with Frank Churchill, has been a curious business. I confess, I had my suspicions, but I did not wish to voice them too strongly, knowing how easily they might be dismissed. And there were circumstances which made it difficult to be certain.”

“I know,” Emma said, her voice soft. “And I, alas, was the foremost in dismissing any notion that did not align with my own preconceived ideas. I am ashamed of my obstinacy, and of my blindness. I see now how much I have yet to learn, how much I need to mend my ways.”

Mr. Knightley looked at her again, and this time, his gaze held a depth of feeling that made Emma’s breath catch. “Emma,” he began, his voice a little lower, “you are very young, and your heart is naturally ardent. To err is human. But to acknowledge one’s errors, to strive for self-improvement, that is the mark of a truly noble character. I have always believed you possessed that nobility, beneath a surface of charming imperfections.”

His words, spoken with such sincerity, so profoundly understanding, brought tears to Emma’s eyes. She could not speak, but merely looked at him, her heart overflowing with a mixture of gratitude, admiration, and a love that she could no longer deny. She wished, with an intensity that surprised her, that she could throw herself into his arms, but propriety, and her own remaining shyness, held her in check.

Mrs. Weston, having finished her letter, now rose and approached them. “Are you two discussing the profound truths of human nature again?” she asked, with a gentle smile. “Mr. Knightley, I must say, your observations are always so very just.”

“We were merely reflecting on the unfortunate events of the past few days, Mrs. Weston,” Mr. Knightley replied, his voice returning to its usual steady tone, though his eyes still held a peculiar warmth as they rested on Emma. “And on the lessons they might teach us.”

The conversation then became more general, and soon after, Mr. Knightley took his leave, promising to call again soon. Emma, however, carried with her the memory of their brief, intimate exchange, and particularly the profound, forgiving gaze he had bestowed upon her. It was a moment that spoke volumes, a silent declaration of understanding and acceptance, and it filled her with a hopeful anticipation for the future.

The ensuing days in Highbury were, as might be expected, dominated by the news from Randalls and Enscombe. The unexpected death of Mrs. Churchill, following so swiftly upon the revelation of Frank Churchill’s engagement, provided a fresh and inexhaustible topic for conversation. Miss Bates, of course, was in her element, perpetually running from house to house, brimming with the latest intelligence, and embellishing it with her own unique blend of enthusiasm and misplaced detail.

“Oh, my dear Miss Woodhouse!” she exclaimed, bursting into Hartfield one morning, scarcely able to contain herself. “Such tidings! Such remarkable events! Poor Mrs. Churchill! Never did I think! And to think, her poor nephew! Such a blow! And Miss Fairfax! Oh, what a situation for her! So happy, and then so sad, all in a breath! And Mr. Weston, quite beside himself, I assure you, for he had always hoped to see his son settled, and now he is, but in such a mournful way! And Mr. Knightley, I assure you, was saying only yesterday, when he called upon us, how very proper it was that the engagement should at last be made public, though he was so sorry for the death, of course, for he is always so very feeling. He said that Miss Fairfax, though delicate, possessed a strength of character that would see her through! And I said, ‘Indeed, Mr. Knightley, you are so right!’”

Emma, though amused by Miss Bates’s effusions, listened patiently, gleaning what she could of the public sentiment. It seemed that, now that the truth was out, general approval, though mingled with commiseration for the bereavement, was settling upon Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax. The mystery and the secretiveness, which had perhaps bred some suspicion, were now replaced by an understanding, however belated, of their difficult circumstances.

Jane Fairfax herself, though still in a state of delicate health and subdued spirits, began to be viewed with a new respect. Her quiet suffering, her steadfastness during the long period of concealed attachment, now became objects of admiration. Emma, visiting her one afternoon, found her pale but composed, bearing her sorrow with a quiet dignity that touched Emma deeply. She offered her sincere condolences for Mrs. Churchill’s death, and expressed her hope that Jane might soon find solace in the open acknowledgment of her engagement.

Jane, with a faint, sad smile, thanked her for her kindness. “It is a strange feeling, Miss Woodhouse,” she said, her voice soft. “To be at once relieved of such a heavy secret, and yet plunged into such a depth of mourning. But I have every confidence that Frank will soon be here, and that, in time, we shall find our happiness.”

Emma felt a genuine warmth for Jane, a feeling untainted by rivalry or past misjudgement. She had wronged Jane in her thoughts, and now, seeing her gentle resignation and quiet fortitude, she wished her every possible happiness.

As the days turned into weeks, Highbury gradually settled into its new understanding of the Churchill-Fairfax engagement. Frank Churchill, though still absent, sent frequent letters to Randalls, filled with expressions of grief for his aunt and eagerness for his return to Highbury and his betrothed. His letters, Mrs. Weston assured Emma, were full of penitence for his past deceptions and gratitude for Jane’s unwavering constancy.

For Emma herself, this period of quiet reflection and gradual change was profoundly transformative. She continued her regular visits to Harriet, whose spirits were slowly, but surely, beginning to revive. The pain of her disappointment in Frank Churchill was fading, replaced by a growing recognition of Emma’s sincere remorse and steadfast friendship. Emma, with a steady hand, gently steered Harriet’s thoughts towards Mr. Martin, and though Harriet remained shy and reticent, Emma perceived a definite thawing in her attitude, a hint that Mr. Martin’s devoted attachment might yet find its reward.

But it was in her relationship with Mr. Knightley that Emma felt the most profound alteration. Their conversations, though often taking place within the larger company of their friends, held a new depth, a subtle understanding that transcended mere words. His eyes, when they met hers, conveyed a trust, a shared perception, and an affection that now thrilled her to her core. She found herself seeking his opinion, valuing his counsel above all others, and delighting in his presence with a quiet joy she had never known.

One afternoon, a few weeks after Mrs. Churchill’s death, Mr. Knightley came to Hartfield. Mr. Woodhouse, enjoying a tranquil nap by the fire, left them, by a happy chance, to themselves. Emma was at her pianoforte, playing a gentle air. She looked up as he entered, a smile naturally gracing her lips.

“You play very sweetly, Emma,” he observed, coming to stand near her. “I have always enjoyed your music.”

“Thank you, Mr. Knightley,” she replied, her heart beating a little faster. “It is a source of much pleasure to me.” She hesitated, then, gathering her courage, looked directly at him. “I have wished for an opportunity to speak with you more fully, Mr. Knightley, without the interruption of others. I wish to express to you, with my whole heart, how deeply I regret my past conduct, and how greatly I have come to value your wisdom, which I so foolishly disregarded.”

Mr. Knightley’s expression softened. He took a seat near her, his gaze steady and warm. “Emma,” he said, his voice low and earnest, “there is no need for such self-reproach. I have seen the change in you, and I have rejoiced in it. Your candour with Harriet, your genuine concern for Jane Fairfax, your very demeanour these past weeks, all speak to a heart that is truly correcting its errors. That is all I have ever wished for you.”

“But I was so ungrateful,” Emma insisted, her voice trembling slightly. “So obstinate, so confident in my own mistaken judgement. I often provoked you, I know, and yet you never ceased to care, never ceased to offer your guidance, however unwelcome it might have been at the time. Your patience, your unwavering goodness, Mr. Knightley, they have always been beyond my desert.”

He reached out and gently took her hand, his touch sending a tremor through her. “Emma,” he said, his voice now even deeper, “you have no idea how much I have valued your spirit, even in its waywardness. I have loved you, Emma, since you were a girl. I have watched you grow, observed your errors with a lover’s anxiety, and longed for your happiness above all else.”
